**The Keeper of Widow’s Point**

The barometer began to fall on the morning of September 12, 1899, and Elias Marlowe did not like the way it fell.

He stood in the lantern room of Widow’s Point Light, a white cylinder of brick and iron set on a spit of sand at the mouth of the inlet, and watched the mercury slide down the glass tube as if it were slipping off a table. The instrument was a brass-and-glass thing, old and temperamental, kept in the watch room below the lamp, and Elias had wound it, cleaned it, and tapped it so many times that he knew its moods as well as he knew the moods of the sea.

It was not a steady fall. It was a sly one.

Outside, the sky had taken on the color of pewter. The sea, which had been running in long, lazy swells
